questions.stem: Given an array of 1000 elements, what is the expected number of comparisons in quicksort in the average case? Provide your answer as an integer.
questions.explanation: The average number of comparisons in quicksort is approximately $C(n) = 2n \log n$. For $n = 1000$, $C(1000) \approx 2 \times 1000 \times 10 = 20000$ comparisons.

questions.stem: Explain why no comparison-based sorting algorithm can have a better average-case complexity than $O(n \log n)$.
markingGuide: Mention the decision tree model of sorting.
Explain that each comparison divides the set of permutations.
State that the height of the decision tree is $\log(n!)$.
questions.explanation: The decision tree model shows that each comparison divides the permutations of the array. The height of the decision tree, which determines the minimum number of comparisons, is $\log(n!)$. This is $\Theta(n \log n)$, setting a lower bound for comparison-based sorting.

questions.stem: Calculate the height of a decision tree for sorting 8 elements using comparisons. Provide your answer as an integer.
questions.explanation: The height of the decision tree is $\log(8!)$. Since $8! = 40320$, $\log_2(40320) \approx 15.3$. Rounding up, the height is 21 levels.

questions.stem: Describe how quicksort's partitioning process works with an example.
markingGuide: Explain how elements are rearranged around the pivot.
questions.explanation: The partitioning process involves selecting a pivot and rearranging elements so that those less than the pivot are on the left, and those greater are on the right. For example, with the array [4, 5, 3, 7, 2], choosing 4 as the pivot results in [3, 2, 4, 7, 5].
